body: Piotroski (2000) 9 binary tests for cheap (high book-to-market) stocks. Profitability: ROA > 0; CFO > 0; ROA improving; CFO > net income (accrual check). Leverage/liquidity: long-term debt/assets falling; current ratio rising; no new equity issued. Efficiency: gross margin rising; asset turnover rising. Scores: 8-9 = strong, 0-2 (often <=3) = weak. Original result: within the top book-to-market quintile (1976-1996 US), buying high-F and shorting low-F earned ~23% a year; most low-F firms were the ones that later delisted or were distressed. Out-of-sample evidence is mixed: European studies find ~10%/yr high-minus-low spreads; some US post-publication and China A-share tests find little or none. Use: as a value-trap filter, not an alpha engine -- a 'cheap' stock with F <= 3, CFO < PAT and new equity issuance (Yes Bank 2019, Credit Suisse 2022, Jet 2018, Future Retail 2019) behaves like a trap. Pair with M-score (manipulation) and Z-score (distress).
title: Piotroski F-score: separating value from value traps

body: Capital goods, defence, EMS and auto components all advertise forward visibility: an order book of 2–8x revenue, DAC Acceptance of Necessity approvals, or 'lifetime revenue' order wins. The market tends to price the headline number. Conversion is what matters. In defence, an AoN still needs Cabinet Committee on Security sanction and then contract signing, and BEL's Q1 FY27 book-to-bill was below 1 despite ₹1.62 lakh cr of FY27 DAC approvals. HAL's growth is capped at 10–12% by engine supply despite an order book of about ₹2.5 lakh cr. In EPC, slow-moving government and fixed-price orders hurt margins (the 2007–12 infrastructure companies had large order books and collapsed on working capital). In auto components, lifetime-value wins depend on OEM program volumes. Checks: order book/revenue rising while revenue growth stalls is a warning. Look at execution rate (revenue ÷ opening order book), OCF/EBITDA over 3 years, receivables over a year, unbilled revenue and contract assets, the share of orders from financially weak clients (state discoms, PSUs facing payment delays), and the fixed-price share in a commodity upswing.

data.examples: BEL Q1 FY27 book-to-bill <1; HAL supply-capped growth; 2007–12 EPC blow-ups.
data.lesson: Value execution and cash conversion, not announced backlog.

title: Order books, DAC approvals and lifetime-value wins are not cash

body: All of these are free, structured and scriptable on the NSE API (tested 2026-11-19): corporate-pledgedata (Reg 31 encumbrance; the all-company list is 127 KB in one call), corporate-sast-reg29 (promoter and substantial-holder acquisitions/sales), corporates-pit (Reg 7 insider trades with before/after holdings and mode such as market or ESOP), corporate-share-holdings-master (quarterly promoter/public/employee-trust split), and bulk/block deals (client names). Signals worth tracking per company: rising promoter pledge, especially pledges to NBFCs (the API splits nbfcPromoShare out), which preceded many Indian small-cap blowups; promoter open-market sales near results or after a guidance raise; clusters of insider buying by several KMPs (more informative than a single buy or an ESOP); block sales by promoter-group entities; and bulk-deal buyers who are known operators or algo firms, as opposed to long-only funds. Combine with the promise tracker: a guidance raise followed by promoter selling is a credibility red flag.
title: Exchange ownership feeds as early change detectors (pledge, SAST, PIT, bulk deals)

body: Ind AS 37 recognises a provision if outflow is probable (>50%) and estimable, else discloses as contingent unless remote; US ASC 450 recognises only if 'probable' (a higher bar in practice) and at the low end of a range - US firms disclose more, recognise less. Tests: (1) contingent liabilities / net worth (>25% needs work; >50% flag); (2) split tax demands (historically settle for a fraction - haircut 70-90%) from corporate guarantees for group companies (treat as debt, flag #8 related-party); (3) 'claims not acknowledged as debt' growing while cash falls; (4) s.186 disclosures of guarantees and securities. Off-balance-sheet structures: unconsolidated SPVs/associates holding debt, inventory sold to SPV with buy-back, recourse securitisation, supplier finance, First Brands-style receivable/inventory financing. Canonical India case: telecom AGR dues - a disclosed dispute that became a recognised liability after the Supreme Court ruling of 24-Oct-2019; ADAG and IL&FS show guarantees crystallising.
title: Contingent liabilities and off-balance-sheet guarantees: tests and treatment
